hero.name: Mehak
hero.who: a 26-year-old graphic designer in Delhi who feels guilty about spending but has no plan

story.b: Mehak earns forty-five thousand a month as a graphic designer in Delhi. Around the twenty-fifth of every month, she opens her bank app and wonders where it all went. Rent, a gym membership she never uses, three streaming apps, late-night online sales. She feels guilty every time she buys a cold coffee near her office in Nehru Place, and sometimes skips it to punish herself. Yet she has never sat down to make a plan. Her savings account holds eleven thousand rupees. Her credit card bill keeps rolling over. A school friend talks confidently about investing, and Mehak nods along, understanding half of it. She feels stingy and broke at the same time.

ask.q: Mehak feels guilty about small treats but has no money plan. What should she do first?
o: Cut out every treat, starting with the cold coffee
Work out what a rich life means to her and build a simple plan around it
Wait for a bigger salary before thinking about money
ask.why: Cutting every treat makes her miserable without fixing the real leaks, and waiting for a raise means the same habits follow the bigger salary. Knowing what she truly values gives her a reason to spend on purpose, which ends the guilt cycle.

chapters.take: Guilt about small spends is not a money plan.

story.b: On Sunday, Mehak sits in her rented room in Lajpat Nagar with a notepad and a cup of tea. She writes down what would make her life feel rich. Not what her colleagues show on Instagram, but what she actually wants. She writes three things. A weekend pottery class she has wanted for two years. Taking her mother from Amritsar on a trip to the hills every summer. Good brushes and paper for her own illustration work. She looks at the list and is surprised. None of it involves designer bags or a fancy car, things she had assumed she should want. For the first time, money feels like a tool for her life rather than a scoreboard.

ask.q: Mehak's colleague thinks being rich means owning what his friends own. What would help him most?
o: Decide what truly makes him happy, and aim his money at that
Buy the same phone and bike as his friends to keep up
Avoid thinking about it and spend as things come
ask.why: Copying friends' purchases chases someone else's idea of success, and spending without thinking leaves him with nothing he values. Deciding what personally makes him happy gives every rupee a direction, and lets him spend on it without guilt.

chapters.take: A rich life means different things to different people. Define yours.

story.b: With her list in hand, Mehak looks at her spending again. She signs up for the pottery class in Hauz Khas and pays for it without a flicker of guilt. She buys the good brushes. Then she cuts hard on things she does not care about. The gym membership she has used twice since March goes. Two of the three streaming apps go. She stops ordering dinner on weekdays out of boredom and cooks a big pot of rajma on Sundays instead. Strangely, she now buys her cold coffee more freely, because she knows it fits the plan. The guilt that used to sit on every small purchase slowly starts to lift.

ask.q: Mehak's flatmate loves travelling but feels guilty about every trip. What advice fits the idea best?
o: Stop travelling until her savings are much bigger
Cut a little from everything equally, including travel
Spend freely on travel and cut hard on the things she does not care about
ask.why: Giving up travel removes the thing she loves most, and equal cuts everywhere leave her with a little less of everything and no real joy. Spending generously on what she loves while cutting hard on the rest ends the guilt and makes her money match her values.

chapters.take: Spend generously on what you love, and cut hard on what you do not.

story.b: Mehak's appraisal is next month. Last year she accepted the first number HR offered, then skipped coffees for months to save a few hundred rupees. This time she does her homework. She asks two designers she trusts what people with three years of experience earn in Delhi. She gathers her best work, including a festive campaign that helped the agency win a big client. She practises what to say with a friend over chai. She also looks hard at her credit card, where the interest has quietly cost her more than all her coffees combined. She clears it with her small savings and promises never to roll it over again. These, Mehak realises, are the amounts that really matter.

ask.q: Mehak's friend wants to save more and plans to skip her daily tea. What would make a bigger difference?
o: Prepare to negotiate her salary and clear any high-interest debt
Skip the tea and also stop meeting friends for meals
Track every rupee spent on snacks in a spreadsheet
ask.why: Skipping tea and tracking snacks save small amounts while adding stress. A better salary or clearing high-interest debt can be worth far more than years of skipped snacks. Putting energy where the amounts are large brings real change.

chapters.take: Put your energy where the amounts are large, not tiny.

story.h: Money that moves on its own
story.b: Mehak's appraisal goes well, and her salary rises. She knows that if the extra money sits in her account, it will quietly disappear into sales. So she sets up a system once. On the second of every month, the day after salary arrives, an automatic transfer sends a fixed amount to a separate savings account for her mother's trip. Rent goes by standing instruction. Her card bill is set to auto-pay in full. Whatever remains is hers to spend, without guilt. In the first month, she forgets the system exists until she sees the savings balance growing. During the Diwali sale, Mehak spends only what is left, and the trip money stays untouched.

ask.q: Her flatmate says she will save whatever is left at the end of the month. What would work better?
o: Promise herself to be extra careful with spending
Save only in months when she feels disciplined
Set an automatic transfer to savings right after salary arrives
ask.why: Whatever is left at month end is usually very little, and promises and disciplined months both depend on willpower. An automatic transfer right after salary arrives moves the money before temptation can reach it, so saving happens even in busy, tired months.

chapters.take: Set your money up to move on its own, and willpower matters less.

story.b: Mehak has wanted to start investing for months. She has watched dozens of reels, read long comment threads and compared funds in a spreadsheet with forty rows. Every week she feels she needs to learn a little more first. Her spreadsheet grows. Her investments stay at zero. One evening, she spends twenty minutes learning how a simple, low-cost index fund works, then sets up a small monthly SIP through her bank app. The amount is modest, and she knows markets can go up and down along the way. It is not perfect, and it does not need to be. She has started, and Mehak realises that matters far more than finding the perfect choice.

ask.q: Mehak's colleague has been comparing funds for six months and still has not started. What should Mehak suggest?
o: Keep researching until he is certain he has found the best fund
Start a small, simple, low-cost plan now and learn as he goes
Pick whichever fund did best last year, since it must be the winner
ask.why: Waiting for certainty can last forever, and last year's top performer makes no promise about next year. A small, simple, low-cost start gets him going, and he can learn and adjust over time. This is general guidance, not personal financial advice.

chapters.take: A simple plan started early beats a perfect plan started late.

story.b: Weeks later, Mehak books train tickets to Dharamshala for herself and her mother in May, paid for from the savings account that filled itself. She does not feel the old guilt. Her pottery class has produced three lopsided bowls that she loves. The credit card balance is zero, and the SIP runs quietly in the background. She does not check it every day. When her school friend talks about money now, Mehak joins in, though she admits she is still learning. She still buys a cold coffee at Nehru Place most afternoons. The difference is that she enjoys it, because she knows where every rupee is going and why.

chapters.take: When money matches your values, spending stops feeling like guilt.
